## Verdict
[INFERENCE] Reusing eval_btc_candles and eval_btc_candle_stats can affect later repetitions if Gina stores tables beyond an MCP connection in a namespace shared by that bearer/account. Neither contamination nor isolation is established by this source review. Clean model chats and native-profile isolation do not prove clean Gina backend data.

## Established behavior
- The fixed names are literal prompt text (perps.yaml:358,378). The repetition loop dispatches the same case object, without a per-repetition name suffix (live.ts:223-234). The two cases use different names; the obvious same-name reuse is across repetitions of each case.
- Creation is documented as materializing bounded fills/candles/depth. Querying must use the successful result’s exact tableName both as query-tool table name and SQL relation—not the requested, sanitized, reconstructed, expired, or cross-user name (SKILL.md:27-34). That instruction permits requested and returned names to differ; it does not guarantee unique names or explain how they are produced.
- A fresh Gina MCP client is acquired inside every runOmpHarnessPluginEvalTrial invocation (omp-harness.ts:1507-1509), used for catalog discovery and that trial’s tools (1513-1542), then closed on exit (1673-1676;1035-1067). Create and query within one trial therefore share that client. There is no cross-trial MCP-client singleton here.
- Each invocation also creates its own model session and uses --no-session (1589;1621-1638). Native agentDirectory is passed to the model process (1601-1604), not as Gina identity.
- Gina transport configuration explicitly supplies the endpoint, Authorization bearer, constant clientName ask-gina-omp-eval, and initialization cancellation signal (1011-1033). Every trial receives the same enclosing credentials.accessToken (bin/live.ts:1508-1517). The wrapper forwards input unchanged after schema validation (1170-1259); it does not inject runId, repetition, case ID, native profile, or model-chat ID into tool arguments. Protocol-managed MCP session headers may exist, but this configuration does not establish how Gina uses them for tables.
- The separate public SDK similarly has no explicit chat/session option. It creates and closes an MCP connection per operation and forwards name/arguments (sdk/client.ts:16-27,80-90; transport.ts:84-158). This is not evidence that server-side tables disappear when a connection closes.

## Precisely unknown
No backend table implementation or concrete table input/output schema was found in the inspected repository client/catalog/plugin slice; the architecture identifies the private application as operating source (ai_docs/architecture.md:3-5). The harness obtains actual input schemas remotely at runtime (omp-harness.ts:1513-1528,1233-1244), and this investigation made no remote API calls.

Unproven: whether duplicate creation rejects, returns existing data, refreshes/replaces, appends, or allocates a fresh name; naming/normalization rules; namespace key (user/account/token/provider/chat/MCP session/global); table TTL and cleanup; whether disconnect deletes tables; concurrent-creation behavior; SQL access enforcement and stale-data behavior. Catalog readOnlyHint/destructiveHint annotations (contracts/index.ts:187-201) do not prove any of these semantics.

## Distinguishing failures using existing evidence
- Name collision: an explicit backend duplicate/already-exists error on a schema-valid create request, tied to the same effective table namespace/name after an earlier successful creation, would be strong distinguishing evidence. A later-repetition failure alone is not enough. Silent stale-table reuse would instead require returned identity/data/provenance evidence; successful routing cannot rule it out.
- Routing failure: absent/wrong tool or wrong sequence is directly distinguishable from observed tool names. However, a failed create can itself prevent the required query, so sequence failure need not originate in model routing.
- Argument failure: host capture code invalid_arguments identifies validation failure before invocation (omp-harness.ts:1189-1194). Wrong-but-schema-valid arguments require inspecting captured arguments. Requested-name misuse requires comparing query arguments/SQL with the actual successful create result.
- Important evidence limit: host observations retain arguments, result byte counts and generic MCP tool call failed errors, not raw successful result bodies or backend error details (1170-1219;1409-1416;1723-1738). Generic tool failure cannot distinguish collision from transport/backend failure. Model final-answer claims alone are not backend proof.
- These two cases have no deterministic argument constraints (perps.yaml:352-391); grading automatically passes that dimension when absent, and routing only checks names/order (grading.ts:84-104,125-130). Therefore an overall routing/argument pass does not itself prove exact returned-tableName usage or isolation.

Source-only inspection; no credentials, run artifacts, model/API calls, tests, builds, edits, or run changes. No runtime idempotency claim.
